listings.name: Edinburgh International Festival
listings.content: The original that spawned all the rest. Founded in 1947 and still seen as more "high-brow" than any of its offspring. Surprisingly, tickets are often priced more reasonably than for many Fringe shows. Some events have preview performances at a much lower price.

listings.name: Edinburgh Military Tattoo
listings.content: One of the iconic images of Edinburgh for millions worldwide is the yearly Tattoo, kilted pipers skirling below the battlements of Edinburgh Castle. Although tickets sell out well in advance, persevering individuals are likely to find one or two tickets still for sale due to cancellations. Just be prepared to ask, ask, and ask again! There are usually fireworks at the end of the shows which can also be seen from e.g. the Grassmarket area.

listings.name: Edinburgh Festival Fringe
listings.content: As the name might suggest, this festival developed on the fringe of the main International Festival and offers more alternative performances, with an emphasis on comedy and avant-garde; it is now the largest arts festival in the world. Many shows offer cheaper preview tickets on the first two days of the festival or a 2-for-1 ticket special on two selected dates. There are a few sub-festivals that are part of the Fringe such as the Assembly Festival, Summerhall Festival and CtheFestival. Part of the Fringe are also many free events (with donation if you liked the show) across the city grouped mostly under the PBH's Free Fringe or Free Festival.

listings.name: Edinburgh Jazz and Blues Festival
listings.content: Festival of about 150 concerts in 11 venues.

listings.name: Edinburgh International Book Festival
listings.content: Takes place in a temporary village of marquees at Charlotte Square Gardens (West End of George Street, New Town).

listings.name: Edinburgh Art Festival
listings.content: Some permanent outdoor commissions which can be seen all year, and temporary exhibitions and events during the festival.

listings.name: Edinburgh Mela
listings.content: Multicultural festival held in Leith.

listings.name: Edinburgh International Television Festival
listings.content: Predominantly a "closed shop" for industry professionals only.

listings.name: Edinburgh International Science Festival
listings.content: Takes place annually in March or April. Emphasis on "hands-on" science.

listings.name: Beltane Fire Festival
listings.content: Fire Festival marking the beginning of summer (evening of April 30). The festival has its origins in the pre-Christian Celtic festival of the same name, which was held to herald the coming of spring and to celebrate the fertility of the countryside. Drums, dancing, semi-nudity, pagan ritual, home-brew and lots of fire and fireworks. Crowds of around 12,000 enjoy the ceremony and spectacle every year. For the full traditional experience stay awake until dawn and head across to Arthurs Seat to wash your face in the dew.

listings.name: Hidden Door
listings.content: Annual non-profit art, music, theatre, etc. event taking place in unused spaces in the city that change from year to year. End of May/beginning of June.

listings.name: Degree Show
listings.content: Around the end of May the Edinburgh College of Art opens its doors and exhibits the works on art, design and architecture of their students. A similar event, the Masters Degree Show, takes place in August as part of the Edinburgh Art Festival. See the ECA event calendar for details.
listings.address: Edinburgh College of Art, Old Town

listings.name: Imaginate Festival
listings.content: Every May/June, an international festival of children's theatre.

listings.name: Meadows Festival
listings.content: A free festival in the Meadows (South) on a weekend in early June with lots of food stalls, second-hand merchandise and live music.

listings.name: Edinburgh International Film Festival
listings.content: Now moved to June from its former slot in August, so that it no longer clashes with all the others! Centred around the Filmhouse Cinema on Lothian Road, though other cinemas take part too. In 2022 it is back in August, but it is not clear if this is a permanent change.

listings.name: Samhuinn Fire Festival
listings.content: Fire Festival marking the beginning of winter (evening of October 31). Procession and enacted fight between the King of Summer and Prince of Winter with great accompanying percussion.

listings.name: Guy Fawkes Night
listings.content: Evening of November 5. With ticketed fireworks (£6.50) in the Meadowbank Sports Centre (East). Can be seen (for free) from several locations in the city.

listings.name: St Andrew's Day
listings.content: Celebrate St Andrew's Day, Scotland's national day on November 30. There are many free events on the nearest weekend in Edinburgh. Historic Scotland opens many of its sites for free (free tickets are required and can be booked online).

listings.name: Dr Neil's Garden
listings.content: Secluded terraced garden on the shores of the loch, behind the church. The Neils were a GP couple who laid out the garden in the 1960s. The little tower, built 1825, is not to ward off body-snatchers but a storage space for the heavy curling stones.

listings.name: Portobello Swim Centre
listings.content: Traditional Victorian baths with pool, gym, sauna and Turkish Baths. Visitors often find the place cold and dirty.

listings.name: Bonoful
listings.content: Reliable place for Indian food.

listings.name: Foresters Guild
listings.content: Good pub fare and cask ales, inside or in one of their beach huts.

listings.name: Malvarosa
listings.content: Good selection of tapas and slick service.

listings.name: The Beach House
listings.content: Right by the beach with sea views, good selection of food.

listings.name: Mouse Hole Deli
listings.content: Good value deli for takeaway food.

listings.name: Cherry's Cafe
listings.content: A small cafe serving Turkish food and breakfast.

listings.name: Sheep Heid Inn
listings.content: 18th-century pub, with implausible claims to date from 1360, and perhaps named for the village slaughter-ground. In 1745 Bonnie Prince Charlie's army camped outside for a month and he held a Council of War here, to good effect as he proceeded to beat Jonny Cope at the Battle of Prestonpans. The skittle alley dates from 1880. The Inn serves good food, with a popular Sunday roast.

listings.name: The Regent
listings.content: LGBT+ and straight-friendly bar with real ale.

listings.name: Abercorn Guest House
listings.content: Pleasant B&B close to the beach. Free parking, no pets.

listings.name: Straven Guest House
listings.content: Friendly small B&B close to the beach. No children under 12 or pets.

listings.name: Seabreeze
listings.content: Friendly spotless B&B east end of the beach.

listings.name: Kings Manor Hotel
listings.content: Friendly comfy mid-price hotel near Brunstane station.

listings.name: The Brae
listings.content: Small welcoming B&B on the A1.

listings.name: Premier Inn Edinburgh East
listings.content: Reliable chain offering, on A1 yet quiet.

listings.name: Royal Yacht Britannia
listings.content: This ship was commissioned in 1954 and was the royal transport and residence on overseas tours until 1997. She has a length of 412 ft / 126 m and oil-fired twin turbines; she was also designed to act as a hospital ship in wartime but was never so used. Symbolically her last duty was to bring home the Governor of Hong Kong after the crown colony was handed over to China, and the last scrap of British Empire was ceded to the rising superpower. She was not replaced, in spite of a rearguard action by the flag-waving political right wing. Princess Diana took her honeymoon cruise aboard with Charles and must have experienced utter heart-sink: the average double-glazing millionaire has a better yacht than this. The royal apartments exhibit all the flair and comfort of the parlour of the deputy headmistress of a genteel boarding school. (See the Fingal Hotel, owned by the Britannia Trust and moored nearby, for what design pizzazz and a big budget can achieve.) Almost 270 crew were needed to sail this vessel, which is more military-meets-cruise-ship than a luxury yacht.
listings.price: Adults £25, students and children 7–21 £17.50. UK taxpayers can Gift Aid their admission

listings.name: Trinity House
listings.content: Stately neo-classical building of 1818 which is now a maritime museum, but only open for special events. It's built over its predecessor of 1560, which in turn was built over a medieval monastic site. The organisation dates back to 1380, when Leith mariners gained the right to levy duty on goods landed at the port; the funds supported sick or aged mariners or their families. They went on to fund lighthouses and to develop training for mariners, which became Leith Nautical College. They invested in real estate and the neighbourhood of Trinity was originally theirs. Other medieval ports copied these arrangements, such as Trinity House in London Deptford from 1514 which became the governing body for English lighthouses, but the Leith version was senior and distinct. A separate body for Scottish lighthouses was established in 1786, now called the Northern Lighthouse Board.

listings.name: Hibernian FC
listings.content: The "Hibs" play soccer in the Premiership, Scotland's top tier. The all-seater stadium, capacity 24,000, is at the south edge of Leith. Hibs have played at Easter Road since 1893; in 2000 the pronounced slope of the ground was levelled out. Their traditional city rivals are Hearts. Buses 1 and 35 run down Easter Road but there are more frequent buses down Leith Walk just west or along London Road (A1) just south.

listings.name: Vue
listings.content: Large multiplex chain cinema showing mainstream films. There's another Vue on Greenside Place at the top of Leith Walk.

listings.name: Word of Mouth Bistro
listings.content: Pleasant small bistro for breakfast or lunch. They have another branch in Morningside.

listings.name: Fishers
listings.content: Quality seafood restaurant in an old watchtower.

listings.name: The Ship on The Shore
listings.content: This smart slick place on the waterfront does excellent seafood.

listings.name: The Kings Wark
listings.content: Waterside tavern founded in 1434 serving good modern cuisine.

listings.name: Domenico's
listings.content: Friendly small trattoria by the harbour.

listings.name: The Roseleaf
listings.content: Friendly relaxed cafe bistro.

listings.name: Old Chain Pier
listings.content: A waterfront bistro.

listings.name: Little Chartroom
listings.content: Bistro with quality Scots cuisine.

listings.name: Ardfern
listings.content: Splendid little licensed cafe.

listings.name: Cilantro
listings.content: Great reviews for this small Indian and Bangladeshi restaurant. BYOB from Sainsbury's opposite.

listings.name: Restaurant Martin Wishart
listings.content: Leith's first Michelin Star, serving very good food especially the tasting menu, but several found it short of the "outstanding" implied by the Star.

listings.name: The Kitchin
listings.content: Established in 2006, Tom Kitchen's Michelin-starred restaurant edges Martin Wishart for consistent high quality.

listings.name: Heron
listings.content: Another outstanding restaurant, try the tasting menu.

listings.name: Dogstar
listings.content: This opened in 2026 and quickly drew great reviews for its modern Scottish cuisine.

listings.name: Teuchters Landing
listings.content: Friendly pub with food in a former cruise liner waiting room. Lots of outside tables by the water so a great choice for a sunny afternoon. They have another branch in the West End.

listings.name: Nobles
listings.content: Elegantly decorated cafe bar with good food.

listings.name: Nauticus
listings.content: Nautical-themed pub with dark panelling, they have beer but are mainly a whisky and cocktail bar. No food.

listings.name: Starbank Inn
listings.content: Fine real ales with a view over the Firth of Forth. Food available.

listings.name: Port of Leith Distillery
listings.content: This converted biscuit factory is a vertical distillery - water is pumped just once up the nine-storey building and gravity does the rest, more efficient than multiple intermediate pumping. There's a rooftop bar, and they market Spanish port and sherry but this is just a side-line until their whisky matures. Sherry barrels imported at Leith were traditionally re-used to mature whisky, imparting a rich complex flavour. It's intended to mature whisky here for 7 years, well beyond the legal minimum 3, so it will be a pricy premium brand when it goes on sale in 2030. Meanwhile the hustle is to sign people up as "analysts", who pay over £500 to receive test samples of immature whisky that wouldn't earn a place on the shelves of Lidl.

listings.name: Lind and Lime Distillery
listings.content: They make gin, named for James Lind the Scottish surgeon who advocated the use of limes to treat and prevent scurvy at sea. In 1747 he conducted the world's first controlled clinical trial, comparing six different remedies for scurvy while aboard HMS Salisbury patrolling the western Channel.

listings.name: The Bonnington
listings.content: Friendly neighborhood pub with bar food.

listings.name: Old Eastway Tap
listings.content: Excellent dog-friendly pub with knowledgeable staff.

listings.name: Scotch Malt Whisky Society
listings.content: Connoisseur whisky-drinkers' private club, with other branches on Queen St and in Glasgow, trying to convey old-money opulence and exclusivity without snootiness and froideur. If you've genuinely got a nose for the good stuff and are in Scotland for an extended period then it's worth buying the annual membership. Otherwise it's just a marketing ploy to wannabes.

listings.name: A-Haven Townhouse Hotel
listings.content: Friendly B&B in a Victorian villa with 14 rooms en-suite. Evening meals available. Free secure car parking.

listings.name: Holiday Inn Express Edinburgh Leith Waterfront
listings.content: Modern and comfortable. Friendly service and good location.

listings.name: Malmaison
listings.content: Pleasant waterfront hotel by the historic harbour, some rooms tired.

listings.name: Ocean Apartments
listings.content: Modern, stylish serviced apartments near Leith harbour outlet. Each has two bedrooms (sleeps 4) and everything you need but the beds are hard.

listings.name: Premier Inn Edinburgh Leith Waterfront
listings.content: Everything you'd expect from this value-for-money chain by Newhaven harbour.

listings.name: Fingal
listings.content: Now permanently moored in Alexandra Dock, MV Fingal was the support vessel for the northern lighthouses. She was built in 1963 and stationed in Oban then Stromness. She retired in 2000 and languished awhile in Falmouth, Cornwall then was converted into a luxury hotel, opened in 2019. With 23 cabins, Fingal gets rave reviews for decor, comfort, service and cuisine. No dogs. Owned by the Royal Yacht Britannia Trust, guests get free tickets for Britannia, which suffers by comparison.

listings.name: Ocean Mist
listings.content: A smaller mid-price version of Fingal, so perhaps it should be called "Ossian Mist". Built in 1919 as a minesweeper but not so used as the war had ended, it was the pleasure yacht of a series of playboys, albeit the Second World War saw it recalled to anti-mine duties. It was brought to Leith in the 1980s as a floating restaurant but fell derelict. In 2018 it was refurbished as a 17 cabin hotel, earning good reviews.

listings.name: Calton Hill
listings.content: This is the stubby crag just east of Princes Street: a short stroll up it commands great views. The "National Monument", a memorial to Scots killed in the Napoleonic Wars, was an attempt to out-do the Parthenon in Athens but the money ran out with only the west facade built. Nelson's Tower was built 1807-16 in the shape of an upturned telescope in honour of the naval hero. A Time Ball on the mast drops at 1PM every day just as the One O'Clock Gun is fired from the castle - this gives a time signal to ships in the Firth before the sound rolls out to them, or it would if not obscured by drizzle and the ships in possession of reliable watches. It was operated by the adjacent City Observatory, superseded in 1896 by the Royal Observatory in the south of the city. City Observatory remained active until 2009 then was refurbished as the Collective Gallery exhibition space for modern art.

listings.name: Old Calton Cemetery
listings.content: Atmospheric Georgian graves, memorials, and funerary ornaments. Memorials include those to the philosopher David Hume (1711-1776), to the Scots who died in the American Civil War, and to the Martyrs of Reform imprisoned or transported for sedition in the 1790s for calling for the right to vote.

listings.name: St Andrew's & St George's West Church
listings.content: Completed in 1784, this is the parish church of the New Town. It's Italianate with an unusual elliptical interior, with an ornate ceiling blending Roman, Pompeian and Scottish elements. The steeple holds Scotland's oldest complete peal of bells, cast in 1788. In 1843 this church was the scene of The Great Disruption, when a third of ministers broke with the Presbyterian Church of Scotland to found their own Free Kirk. St George's Church was part of the breakaway, but there was a reconciliation in the 20th century, and in 2013 that congregation merged here. The Undercroft Cafe has homemade food M-F 10:30AM-2PM.

listings.name: Scott Monument
listings.content: Sir Walter Scott (1771-1832) re-invented Scotland. In the late Georgian era, he popularised tales of its medieval and Jacobean tumults, and created the clan tartans you buy on Princes St. This grand Gothic memorial, part cathedral part moon rocket, was completed in 1846 to dominate the east end of Princes St. It's 200 ft 6 in / 61.1 m tall, and guided tours take you up 287 steps (no lift) to the top platform, for a closer look at many of the statuettes of characters from Scott's works. The man himself and his dog sit in state at the base. In the 1990s the curators considered cleaning the monument but realised that the Victorian grime was holding it together, so replacement stonework is prominently white.

listings.name: Royal Scottish Academy
listings.content: An august neo-classical building on The Mound, fronting onto Princes St, and its main function is to be confused with the National Gallery behind. The RSA is a separate organisation promoting contemporary Scottish art. The building hosts temporary exhibitions but doesn't have a permanent display - the Academy's extensive collection is dispersed across many galleries. That might include your own home, as they run an art rental scheme.

listings.name: National Galleries of Scotland: National
listings.content: This holds much of Scotland's fine artwork from Renaissance to 20th century, with changing exhibitions. These rotate seasonally, so an exhibition put on for the Festival typically stays to the end of the year, allowing quieter times to view. Enter from the plaza between gallery and Royal Scottish Academy, and a basement passage connects the two exhibition spaces. The Scottish Galleries on the lowest floor reopened in 2023 after several years of redevelopment, and show a good collection of local work and views which may inspire trips.
listings.price: Free, charges for major temporary exhibitions

listings.name: National Galleries of Scotland: Portrait
listings.content: Completed in 1890, this is a striking red sandstone neo-Gothic building. It holds portraits of Scots from down the ages, with new faces being added all the time: Billy Connolly and Tilda Swinton mingle with Mary Queen of Scots. The entrance hall has a grand frieze of notable Scots in procession.

listings.name: Palestine Museum
listings.content: A branch of their main museum in Woodbridge Connecticut, this is mostly artwork with exhibitions on the Nakhba and other events.

listings.name: Princes Street Gardens
listings.content: The west portion fills the valley beyond the Mound, spanning the railway tracks to the foot of castle crag. The east portion is the terrace around the Scott Monument. They were laid out in the 1820s as private gardens for residents of the street: occupants of bath chairs required a medical certificate that their condition was not contagious. Their initial opening to the public was solely at Christmas and New Year, in the belief that this would distract people from the pubs and reduce drunkenness. In 1876 they became a public park and were re-landscaped and dotted with statues. By this time the gardens were already bisected by railway tracks, the price that had to be paid to finally link the east and west railway terminuses. The gardens are open 24 hours.

listings.name: The Georgian House
listings.content: This townhouse was designed by Robert Adam, completed in 1796 and has been furnished in the style of its first owner John Lamont. Its last private owner the Marquess of Bute also acquired adjacent townhouses and along with the other owners got the entire north facade of the square restored to Adams' imposing original design. Visit by self-guided tour, and in mid-summer you need to book as it sells out.

listings.name: Charlotte Square
listings.content: In front of the house is the mirror-image of St Andrew's Square at the east end of George St. Bute House at Number 6, next door to The Georgian House, is the official residence of the First Minister of Scotland, so you might see a motorcade, TV cameras and armed security outside. The gardens in the square are private. Prince Albert stands in the middle, with his view down the street somewhat impeded by mature trees.

listings.name: Gilbert the Phone Box
listings.content: An old red phone box has been kitted out with Edwardian memorabilia, and nicknamed for Sir Giles Gilbert Scott (1880-1960) designer of the box. You can look in the windows anytime, or collect the key for £3 (for Save the Children) from Stewart Christie and Co who run a long established gentleman's outfitter in the shop next to it.

listings.name: James Clerk Maxwell's Birthplace
listings.content: Isaac Newton realised that what caused the apple to fall was the very same force moving the moon, planets and stars. James Clerk Maxwell (1831-1879) was born in this house, before the family moved to Kirkcudbright. He was intensely curious about how nature worked and made a "great unification" of equal importance to Newton's: that magnetism, electricity, light and heat are all manifestations of the same electromagnetic spectrum. And this spectrum must contain other frequencies beyond human sensing: hence X-rays and radio waves, and the entire science of telecommunications. He made possible Einstein's 20th century unification of gravity, mass and energy, and contributed to many other fields of enquiry. The Foundation has preserved this townhouse with his memorabilia. His statue stands at the east end of George St and a laboratory block is named for him on the Edinburgh University science campus.

listings.name: Dean Village
listings.content: It is an attractive hamlet down in the dene - the steep valley - of the Water of Leith. It was the medieval crossing point on the route from Edinburgh to South Queensferry, and is the main access point for this section of the Water of Leith Walkway (described below). The fast-descending stream drove 11 grain mills here, so it was the powerbase for the Baxters, the bakers' merchant guild. The present bridge across the stream was built in the 18th century, only just wide enough for a horse and cart. The village declined in the 19th century when bigger flour mills were built at Leith, and bypassed in 1833 when Telford's Dean Bridge spanned the valley; the Belford Bridge was added upstream in 1887. Dean village therefore never developed modern roads or industry, so its charming core was preserved.

listings.name: Dean Bridge
listings.content: is best seen from below in Dean Village as you follow the walkway along the stream - from the top it's just a busy thoroughfare. Crossing in four arches 107 ft / 32 m above the stream, it was Telford's last major project. As well as improving the route to Fife, it made the north bank into prime real estate, so elegant terraces were built there.

listings.name: National Galleries of Scotland: Modern One
listings.content: The original modern art gallery, established in 1960, was in the Botanic Gardens. In 1895 it moved into this neoclassical building, originally a refuge for fatherless children, and in 1999 it expanded across the road into the neoclassical orphanage now known as Modern Two. The gardens of Modern One have been sculpted. Both buildings have extensive contemporary collections and most visitors find that seeing one of them is plenty for an afternoon.

listings.name: Modern Two
listings.content: Opposite side of Belford Rd has a slightly smaller collection, but enough to infuriate about one-in-five reviewers, who rage that their kids' drawings stuck on the fridge door are better. A neon sign in the garden reassures all and sundry that "There will be no miracles".
listings.image: Modern Two (Dean Gallery), 73 Belford Road, Edinburgh (side view).jpg

listings.name: St Mary's Episcopal Cathedral
listings.content: This stonking great neo-Gothic church was completed in 1879, designed by Sir George Gilbert Scott, with the towers added in 1917. It's the senior Episcopal church in Scotland, within the Anglican tradition of bishops (and much else) that the Presbyterians rejected. It has daily choral services: the song school (open occasionally) has stunning murals by Phoebe Anna Traquair.

listings.name: St Mary's Metropolitan Cathedral
listings.content: The Roman Catholic Cathedral was established as a chapel in 1814 and became a cathedral in 1886 for the archdiocese of Edinburgh and St Andrews. It was designed by James Gillespie Graham in neo-perpendicular style and has undergone several alterations and extensions - in the 1970s the tenements that hemmed it in were demolished. There are services twice daily in English and daily in Polish.

listings.name: Sherlock Holmes
listings.content: His creator Sir Arthur Conan Doyle (1859-1930) was born nearby at 11 Picardy Place, to a genteel but impoverished Irish Catholic family. His first Sherlock story was published in 1886. The statue was in storage while the plaza was remodelled around the tramlines but restored in June 2023.

listings.name: Edinburgh Playhouse
listings.content: Built as a cinema in 1929 and refurbished in 1980, this is now Scotland's largest performance space, with a capacity of 3059. That's about 1000 more than can comfortably be seated and 2000 more than they have toilet provision for. It's run by ATG, Ambassador Theatre Group.

listings.name: Vue
listings.content: Large multiplex cinema showing mainstream releases.

listings.name: Snax
listings.content: A small fast-food joint, limited seating. The food is cheap and edible, with a decent vegetarian selection.

listings.name: Cafe Piccante
listings.content: Unashamed specialists in late-night greasy food, friendly staff and a DJ at weekends. The burgers are a stand-out and deep-fried mars bars are available for tourists.

listings.name: Cafe Royal
listings.content: Beautifully tiled Victorian palace of a pub, designed in 1862 as a showroom for the latest fixtures and fittings, no dogs. The stylish restaurant serves seafood and other classics.

listings.name: Dishoom
listings.content: Scottish outpost of a small national chain, modelling their interiors on colonial Bombay cafes. The food is made to share, mostly consisting of small plates, with the house chaat, black daal and salli botti particularly memorable. Often busy, but they can usually squeeze you in, remember those Bombay buses and commuter trains.

listings.name: The Dome
listings.content: Bar and grill in a former bank headquarters with grand exterior and impressive interior.

listings.name: Pizza Pilgrims
listings.content: This Neapolitan-style chain pizzeria opened its Edinburgh outlet in 2025 to much hype. It's good not great.

listings.name: Mussel Inn
listings.content: Seafood restaurant owned by shellfish producers, ingredients direct from the west coast.

listings.name: Dulse
listings.content: This serves excellent Scottish seafood.

listings.name: Teuchters
listings.content: Lively pub serving modern Scottish cuisine at reasonable prices.

listings.name: Café Marlayne
listings.content: Chic cosy French bistro serving up excellent French cuisine.

listings.name: Cafe St Honoré
listings.content: Great continental food and wine. Gluten free and dairy free menus available.
listings.address: Thistle Street North West Lane EH2 1EA

listings.name: Contini
listings.content: Restaurant in a former grand banking hall serving wonderful Italian food.

listings.name: Holy Cow
listings.content: Excellent basement vegan cafe. Home-made food.

listings.name: The Palmerston
listings.content: Chicly decorated restaurant and bakery in a former bank, the menu changes daily.

listings.name: Voodoo Rooms
listings.content: Over-the-top decor in this quirky pub, sometimes has live entertainment, mixed reviews for the food.

listings.name: All Bar One
listings.content: Chain pub with slick service and good ale and meals.

listings.name: Eastside
listings.content: Busy cocktail bar and night entertainment spot.

listings.name: The Standing Order
listings.content: A cavernous converted bank building. It's part of the JD Wetherspoon chain and always has a wide range of inexpensive drinks and pub food.

listings.name: Tonic
listings.content: A great cocktail bar with friendly helpful staff.

listings.name: The Oxford Bar
listings.content: Trad drouthy Scottish pub, often a setting in the Ian Rankin "Inspector Rebus" novels.

listings.name: The Kenilworth
listings.content: Splendidly tiled and wood-panelled pub.

listings.name: Mathers
listings.content: Traditional bar with a good range of real ales and whisky, reasonable pub food. Big screen for football and rugby.

listings.name: The Basement
listings.content: Nowadays specialising in Mexico, so this is the place for tequila or tacos.

listings.name: Barony Bar
listings.content: Trad pub, dog-friendly, sometimes has live music. It calls itself a gastropub but customers don't much rate the food.

listings.name: The Cask & Barrel
listings.content: This often features in the novels of Christopher Brookmyre as the pub where journalist "Jack Parlabane" gets tip-offs from the police. The Cask is a proper boozer with a wide selection of Real Ale plus draft and bottled lagers and whisky. Great place to watch football or rugby as they have half a dozen TV screens.

listings.name: The Cumberland Bar
listings.content: Readers of Alexander McCall Smith's 44 Scotland Street will recognise this literary haunt. It's a traditional pub popular with New Town locals, students, the suits from local offices, pretty much everyone in fact. Gets very busy in summer thanks to its lovely beer garden - one of the few central pubs to have one. Plenty of drink options and decent food.

listings.name: Edinburgh Gin Distillery
listings.content: Micro-distillery producing gin in various styles. In summer 2024 they plan to move to larger premises on Market St near the station.

listings.name: easyHotel.com Edinburgh
listings.content: Tiny rooms, but right in the heart of the city facing the castle and Princes Street Gardens. Some rooms have no window.

listings.name: Edinburgh Central Youth Hostel
listings.content: Large hostel near the top of Leith Walk, about 10 minutes walk from Waverley Station. It serves meals and the cafe is open to the public. There is also a self-catering kitchen, and plasma screens abound. In addition to dormitories, some rooms (including singles) are available.

listings.name: ibis Styles St Andrew Square
listings.content: Good value Accor chain hotel 100 yards from the bus station.

listings.name: Premier Inn Edinburgh City Centre (York Place)
listings.content: Reliable chain hotel with spacious rooms for the price, and a/c. Some rooms have views over the New Town and Forth.

listings.name: Cityroomz
listings.content: Bright modern place at the west end of Princes St.

listings.name: B+B Edinburgh
listings.content: Traditional hotel with lovely views, but the lift is chronically out of action.

listings.name: Tigerlily
listings.content: Jazzy hotel near Charlotte Square, spacious rooms. No dogs.
Restaurant in a Georgian town house with four rooms. No dogs.

listings.name: The Hoxton
listings.content: The former Grosvenor re-opened in 2025, so it's sparkling fresh and eager to please.

listings.name: Parliament House Hotel
listings.content: Quiet backwater off busy streets at the foot of Calton Hill. Comfy and great value, tiny bathrooms.

listings.name: Number 11
listings.content: Slick welcoming hotel with great dining.

listings.name: Waldorf Astoria Edinburgh
listings.content: Grand hotel presiding over the west end of Princes St, facing the castle. It was built as the terminus station and hotel for the Caledonian Railway, vying with the rival North British terminus at the east end, now Waverley. The latter became the definitive city terminus, the west end station was demolished in 1970 and "The Caley" was able to expand. Citizens also discovered that it was rose pink, when 70 years of grime was scrubbed off. It earns good but not great reviews for comfort, service and dining in its three restaurants. The property is now owned by an Abu Dhabi holding company but continues to be operated by Hilton.

listings.name: InterContinental The George Hotel
listings.content: 249-room hotel on busy George Street. The hotel was built as townhouses in the 1780s and knocked through into a hotel in 1881. Great scores for comfort, service and location.

listings.name: Old Waverley Hotel
listings.content: Very central location, but poky old rooms and no lift.

listings.name: Balmoral Hotel
listings.content: This baronial pile opened in 1902 as the terminus and hotel of the North British Railway, just pipping the rival Caledonian at the other end of Princes St. Its landmark clock tower is always three minutes fast to speed dawdlers towards their train. The NB Hotel was rebuilt to become the Balmoral in 1990. Great service and trad ambience, some visitors found it dated.

listings.name: Nira Caledonia
listings.content: Hotel (more like a B&B) at the edge of Stockbridge. Tiny rooms and beds, tall guests will suffer.

listings.name: Kimpton Charlotte Square Hotel
listings.content: On a charming garden squares, this 199-room was seven inter-connecting Georgian townhouses, built in 1791 to a design by Robert Adam, and converted to a hotel in 1881.

listings.name: Cheval Edinburgh Grand
listings.content: Plush studios and apartments between railway and bus stations.

listings.name: The Glasshouse
listings.content: Comfy central hotel, service spasmodic.

listings.name: Edinburgh Castle
listings.content: Iconic fortress perched magnificently on a volcanic rock above the city. The castle has been continuously used for 1100 years and is kept in excellent condition; it's still the ceremonial headquarters of the army in Scotland. Highlights include the Great Hall, the Honours of Scotland (the Scottish Crown Jewels), the War Museum and the 12th century St Margaret's Chapel. The One O'Clock Gun is fired each day from Mills Mount battery. Audio guides available. It's mobbed with tourists and in summer often sells out, book online well in advance.
listings.price: Adult £19.50, child (7-15) £11.40, conc £15.50, Historic Scotland / English Heritage / Cadw free

listings.name: Camera Obscura
listings.content: Over 150 years old, the Camera Obscura projects light from the top of the tower onto a large dish in a dark room below, displaying a panorama of the city. The effect still works on overcast days or at night but is best in sunlight, when you can use a sheet of paper to "pick up" people seen in the streets and have them scurry in your hand. The tower also houses a gallery of optical illusions that wouldn't be out of place in Blackpool.

listings.name: Gladstone's Land
listings.content: Thomas Gladstone was a wealthy merchant, and in 1617 he had this house refashioned to accommodate his family and to partly rent out. A "Land" means a tall narrow townhouse from the period when Old Town was cramped and the only space for development was upwards. Typically along the Royal Mile the ground floor was shops and trade, genteel folk lived on the first and second floors, and lower-income residents had to lump up many steps to the upper floors. It's now a museum run by the National Trust for Scotland exhibiting 17th century elite city life, richly furnished and decorated but with no running water. In the 18th century prosperous folk relocated to New Town, where the NTS property at 7 Charlotte Square continues the story.
listings.price: Adult £10, conc £8.50, child £6, NTS / NT free

listings.name: Writers' Museum
listings.content: This museum, in a tall house built in 1622, celebrates three Scottish literary giants: Robert Burns, Sir Walter Scott and Robert Louis Stevenson. From 1719 the close was the residence of the widow of the 1st Earl of Stair, who ordered the Glencoe massacre.

listings.name: St Giles
listings.content: It's often called a Cathedral, but the Church of Scotland brooks no such episcopal entity, and Charles I dubbing it "cathedral" in 1633 was one reason his head was chopped off. Safer to call it "High Kirk", though they're nowadays lenient with first time offenders. The present building is from 14th century with much Victorian Gothic, notably its crowned spire. Highlight is the Chapel of the Order of the Thistle, Scotland's chivalric company of royal knights. Services are M-F at noon and 9:30AM and 11AM on Sunday, with choral music at 6PM.

listings.name: Mary King's Close
listings.content: Mary King (1590-1644) was a clothes merchant and city burgess. She died the year before plague struck and carried off the rest of her family. In 1753 Royal Exchange, now City Chambers, was built over several closes by demolishing their upper storeys, while the lower storeys were used for storage then later blocked off. This means a warren of medieval alleys and low dwellings has been preserved, re-opened in 2003 and visited by guided tour. Almost as weighty as the Exchange is the mass of ghost stories piled on top of the close, woo-ooh! - but the real history is fascinating enough. Book ahead as it often sells out.

listings.name: Museum of Childhood
listings.content: Concepts and imagery of childhood are ever-changing. See if you can find your (or your grandparents') old toys in the collection, and your place in history.

listings.name: The Peoples' Story Museum
listings.content: This is housed in Canongate Tolbooth, the medieval centre for governance and justice (preferably gruesome) as Canongate was a separate jurisdiction until 1856. The museum covers the story of working class life, and of organised labour, from the late 18th century to the present.

listings.name: Canongate Kirk
listings.content: In 1687 James VII (II of England) chucked the Protestants out of Holyrood to convert it to a royal Roman Catholic chapel, the sort of behaviour that got him ousted from the monarchy the following year. The congregation moved to Infirmary St then to this building on its completion in 1691. From 1952 Queen Elizabeth II regularly attended when at Holyrood, and in 2011 her granddaughter Zara Phillips married former England rugby captain Mike Tindall here. Notables in its graveyard include George Drummond (1788-1866) co-founder of the New Town, poet Robert Fergusson (1750–1774), and economist Adam Smith (1723-90). Memorials also commemorate soldiers dying at Edinburgh Castle, for which this was the graveyard, and coachmen of the London-Edinburgh stagecoach, which had its terminus here.

listings.name: Museum of Edinburgh
listings.content: Museum of city history in a mustard-hued mansion built in 1570.

listings.name: Dunbar's Close Garden
listings.content: This close was re-modelled in the 1970s to recreate a 17th-century physic and knot garden, a hidden quiet place in the busy city.

listings.name: Scottish Parliament
listings.content: A unique building, designed by Spanish Catalan architect Enric Miralles, completed in 2004. It's either a daring showpiece of postmodern architecture or a national embarrassment or a bit of both, time will tell. Parliament meets Tu-Th and you can watch debates from the Public Gallery, ask for tickets at reception. First Minister's Question Time is normally Th noon-12:45PM, and you need to reserve this up to 7 days in advance. Waiting list places may be available from 10AM on the day, otherwise watch from the Overspill Room. On non-business days (M F Sa) you can view the debating chamber from the Public Gallery without tickets. In the lobby area there are often exhibitions.

listings.name: Dynamic Earth
listings.content: Interactive natural history museum exhibiting the forces and features of our planet: volcanoes, polar ice, rainforests and so on. Opened in 1999, it's a tent-like structure on the former site of a gasworks and brewery.

listings.name: Holyrood Palace
listings.content: The Palace is a royal residence, closed when the king is here for a week in July and for similar state occasions. It's been repeatedly smashed up and rebuilt, and the present building is mostly from the 1670s. Highlights are the grand stair, state apartments, throne room, Mary Queen of Scots Chambers (where bloodstains from the murder of Rizzio are still visible), King's Gallery a sample of the royal art collection, the ruin of Holyrood Abbey, and the palace gardens.

listings.name: George IV Bridge
listings.content: This high-level road courses south from the top of High Street and spans the hollow of Grassmarket. Completed in 1836, it's lined with Victorian and modern buildings such as the two libraries. Victoria Street descends into the hollow, while Victoria Terrace is a walkway above it that loops back onto Royal Mile.

listings.name: National Library of Scotland
listings.content: A venerable reference library, which you need membership to access, but it has public exhibitions about literature. "Treasures" is its permanent exhibition. But don't stumble in here mistaking it for Central Library across the street.

listings.name: Central Library
listings.content: See Edinburgh#Connect for how to access. The internet stations are in the Learning Centre, and the building houses Central Lending Library, Central Reference Library, Central Children's Library, Edinburgh and Scottish Collections, Art & Design Library and Music Library. It has a wealth of material for research such as old newspapers and maps, but births, marriages and deaths are filed at East Register House by the bus station in New Town.

listings.name: Greyfriars Kirk
listings.content: This church was built in 1620 on the grounds of an abandoned Franciscan Friary, but seriously damaged by later calamities or Acts of God so the present structure is mostly Victorian. It remains active, as other Presbyterian churches have closed and their congregations moved here. The main visitor interest is the ancient graveyard: notable denizens include the architects William and John Adam, the notorious hell-rake Colonel Charteris, Captain Porteous lynched after he fired on rioters, William McGonagall the worst poet in Scotland, and Greyfriars Bobby plus his owner. The mortsafe kept coffins locked until burial, else the body-snatchers would make off with them.

listings.name: National Museum of Scotland
listings.content: Superb museum of Scotland's heritage. You enter into the lofty Victorian Grand Gallery, where the millennium clock chimes on the hour. Exhibition halls cover Scottish and world history and culture, science, technology, art and design, and natural history. Dolly the sheep, the 12th-century Lewis chess pieces, and dinosaurs are some of the highlights. NMS also run the War Museum in the castle, the Museum of Flight near Gullane, and the Museum of Rural Life in East Kilbride.

listings.name: Anatomical Museum
listings.content: Large collection of anatomical specimens and life and death masks. Best known is the skeleton of William Burke, hanged in 1829 after he and William Hare killed at least 16 people to sell the bodies for dissection. Limited opening as the area is in continual use for teaching, booking essential.
listings.address: Doorway 3, Medical School, Teviot Place EH8 9AG

listings.name: St Cecilia's Hall
listings.content: Scotland's oldest purpose-built concert hall, opened in 1763 and still in regular use. It hosts the University of Edinburgh collection of historic musical instruments, crafted 16th to 20th century, many of which (such as the Trompette Demilune) are no longer played.

listings.name: Talbot Rice Gallery
listings.content: David Talbot Rice (1903-72) was in the louche crowd at Oxford that inspired Brideshead Revisited and became a distinguished scholar of East Mediterranean and Russian art, with extensive contacts in those parts - how come this fellow was never implicated in a spy ring? His spell as University Vice Principal is commemorated in this gallery with changing exhibitions of contemporary art. It's housed within Old College of Edinburgh University, a fine building built between 1789 and 1827 by Robert Adam and Henry Playfair. The Georgian Gallery has a Playfair interior and a mixture of Old Masters and modern installations.

listings.name: Dovecot Studios
listings.content: Tapestry studio and gallery housed in the former public baths. There is a cafe, shop, and viewing gallery where you can look down on weavers at work.

listings.name: Surgeons' Hall Museums
listings.content: The permanent exhibitions are the Pathology Museum, the History of Surgery and the Dental Museum. Not suitable for children under 10 as the exhibits include human remains.

listings.name: Edinburgh Central Mosque
listings.content: Stately mosque and minaret completed in 1998 in a modern variant of Turkish style. You can generally look in between prayer times.

listings.name: City Art Centre
listings.content: Four-floor gallery run by the city council. They rotate artwork from their extensive Scottish collection and have changing exhibitions.

listings.name: Fruitmarket
listings.content: Gallery of contemporary art, refurbished in 2018. From 1936 to the 1970s this was where soft fruit and veg were traded, handy for the trains and delivery vans.

listings.name: Stills
listings.content: Photography gallery with three exhibitions a year. They also support photographers through courses and hire of equipment, darkroom and digital lab.

listings.name: Museum on the Mound
listings.content: Museum about money and coins, in the basement of the Palladian pile of the former Bank of Scotland headquarters. Scotland developed a banking sector in the 18th century to support long-distance trade, and still prints its own banknotes.

listings.name: The Edinburgh Dungeon
listings.content: "Haunted House" experience, where you take a 70 min tour through 11 shows and 2 rides loosely based on Scotland's horrible history: William Wallace, Mary King's Ghost, cannibal Sawney Bean, Burke and Hare and more.

listings.name: Escape The Past
listings.content: Immersive escape rooms and outdoor puzzle trails based on Edinburgh's history. Experiences include historically accurate props, live actors and special effects. Housed in the basement of a 19th Century Methodist Church. Highlights include "The Anatomist" a 60 minute escape room based on Edinburgh's grave-robbing-era medical history.

listings.name: The Scotch Whisky Experience
listings.content: Tour of the history and craft of whisky distilling, with expert guides - the basic or "silver" tour works well for beginners. They have a huge selection; the core of it is the 3384 bottles collected by Brazilian whisky enthusiast Claive Vidiz.

listings.name: The Lost Close
listings.content: Underground experiences and tours led by expert Storytellers. Whisky, gin and beer tastings available - starting from £15.

listings.name: Monkey Barrel Comedy
listings.content: Intimate comedy venue with several acts each night. Drink and some food available.

listings.name: Festival Theatre
listings.content: Large performance venue, home of the Scottish Ballet and Scottish Opera. It also hosts contemporary dance, ballet, musicals and panto.

listings.name: Reid Concert Hall
listings.content: General Reid (1721-1807) endowed the School of Music at the University of Edinburgh. They put on occasional free lunchtime concerts here, especially on 13 Feb, Reid's birthday. You may also be able to look in on their collection of antique instruments.

listings.name: Usher Hall
listings.content: The city's main concert hall, capacity 2200, and home to the Royal Scottish National Orchestra. It was completed in 1914, funded by Andrew Usher the whisky distiller and blender.

listings.name: Royal Lyceum
listings.content: Completed in 1883 and little altered since, this is home to the Royal Lyceum Theatre Company.

listings.name: Traverse Theatre
listings.content: Since 1992 this has hosted Traverse theatre company, dedicated to new works.

listings.name: King's Theatre
listings.content: Reopened in August 2026 after 4 years of refurbishment.

listings.name: Cameo Cinema
listings.content: Mainstream, arthouse and alternative films, with an Edwardian interior.

listings.name: Odeon Cinema
listings.content: Mostly mainstream movies.

listings.name: The Piemaker
listings.content: This has a wide range of delicious pies and savoury pastries, piping hot. They're mostly a takeaway and don't deliver, but have a few seats inside.

listings.name: Kebab Mahal
listings.content: Good halal curries, kebabs and tandooris, no alcohol.

listings.name: The Original Mosque Kitchen
listings.content: Inexpensive chicken or vegetable curry. A favorite with generations of Edinburgh University students for its cost and portion sizes.

listings.name: Tempting Tattie
listings.content: Inexpensive takeaway for trad baked potatoes.

listings.name: Kampong Ah Lee
listings.content: Tasty Malaysian dishes such as Roti Canai, Satay, Nasi Lemak, Laksa and Rendang.

listings.name: Em’s Kitchen
listings.content: Full Scottish breakfast, shakshuka, coffee and tea options, with seating that looks into a quiet car park and garden.

listings.name: John's Coffee House & Tavern
listings.content: Located in a historic building. Breakfast, all-day waffles, light lunch options, small plates to share, bar with wide range of Scotch whiskies.

listings.name: The Everest
listings.content: Good inexpensive Nepalese and Indian food.

listings.name: Petit Paris
listings.content: Traditional French restaurant complete with chequered tablecloths and whitewashed walls.

listings.name: David Bann
listings.content: Imaginative and tasty vegetarian food, with lots available for vegans or GF.

listings.name: Whiski
listings.content: A bit touristy, but a good choice for Scottish food, drink and music. Hundreds of whiskies available, bar staff happy to advise. Live music every night from 9:30PM, try to sit up front for this.

listings.name: Nok's Kitchen
listings.content: Decent Thai food with vegetarian options. They add 10% service to the menu prices.

listings.name: Kanpai Sushi
listings.content: Small portions of sushi and other Japanese food, and pricey, but speedy service and memorable quality.

listings.name: Gurkha
listings.content: Traditional Indian and Nepalese restaurant.

listings.name: Kalpana
listings.content: Long-established quality vegetarian Indian restaurant serving curries, thalis and tandooris.

listings.name: Tanjore
listings.content: One of the few places in Edinburgh serving South Indian food such as Dosas, Uttapams, Sambar and other Tamil specialities.

listings.name: MUMS
listings.content: Classic British comfort food: haggis, fish & chips, sausage & mash, stews, or shepherd's pie. Lots of veggie choices, no reservations.

listings.name: The Elephant House
listings.content: Consistently good coffee and light bites, cafe is full of university and creative types; JK Rowling wrote much of the first Harry Potter book here. And that alas is the problem: it's become part of the Potter circus, every half hour sees another coachload of tourists all craning for selfies and trying to nick the cutlery and scrawling graffiti in the loo. Prices, service and ambience have suffered accordingly, and Rowling has fled to a castle in the Highlands. In Aug 2021 the cafe suffered a fire and was closed for 5 years.

listings.name: The Witchery by the Castle
listings.content: By the castle entrance, The Witchery serves top-class food in an elegant candle-lit restaurant. They've now added rooms, flamboyantly camp.

listings.name: Timberyard
listings.content: Outstanding Scottish cuisine in a 19th century warehouse, with extensive wine list. One Michelin star, the head chef is Jimmy Murray.

listings.name: The Jolly Judge
listings.content: Cosy independent pub with a good selection of beer and whisky. One of the few pubs on Royal Mile that's not a tourist trap.

listings.name: Albanach
listings.content: Cosy Belhaven pub with food and whisky.

listings.name: Doctors
listings.content: Now a Belhaven pub, this is a welcoming place with good ales and food. It was a few yards from the former Royal Infirmary, within bleep range and sprinting distance for the junior doctors.

listings.name: Sandy Bells
listings.content: Likewise frequented by medical students, this has live folk music every night.

listings.name: The Pear Tree
listings.content: Popular with students, this has a large beer garden and outdoor big screen for TV sports.

listings.name: The Kilderkin
listings.content: Fair selection of cask ales and whisky, the food is so-so and the warmth of welcome varies. This is the original of a chain that now includes The Windsor on Elm Row, Blue Blazer on Spittal St and Bennets at Tolcross.

listings.name: The Bow Bar
listings.content: Old-style boozer with a large selection of whiskies, selection of guest ales, and no background music.

listings.name: Bennets Bar
listings.content: A good old-fashioned pub, now part of Kilderkin group, with a wide selection of real ale and whisky. It is traditionally the place for pre / post-theatre drinks, with the Kings Theatre.

listings.name: The Bongo Club
listings.content: A café-bar and live music venue.

listings.name: Cabaret Voltaire
listings.content: Atmospheric basement vault with regular gigs.

listings.name: Dragonfly
listings.content: Well-hidden but popular cocktail lounge.

listings.name: The Jazz Bar
listings.content: Live music every night, majoring on jazz; early shows are generally free, later gigs individually priced. Limited food or seating.

listings.name: The Liquid Room
listings.content: 800-capacity live music venue.

listings.name: Wash Bar
listings.content: Modern pub, mostly a local crowd, TV sport, no food.

listings.name: 56 North
listings.content: Cocktail bar incorporating South Loch gin distillery.

listings.name: Motel One Edinburgh Royal
listings.content: Comfy efficient place by the station, great value. They have another branch by the bus station.

listings.name: Kick Ass Greyfriars
listings.content: Cheerful friendly staff and modern amenities. Offers dormitory beds and 2-4 bed private rooms.

listings.name: Code The Court
listings.content: Hybrid hostel/hotel in a former jail and courtroom. Offers pod capsules and private rooms.

listings.name: Castle Rock Hostel
listings.content: Clean spacious hostel with 300 beds on the hill just below Castle Esplanade.

listings.name: ibis Edinburgh Centre South Bridge
listings.content: Reliable chain hotel.

listings.name: ibis Edinburgh Centre Royal Mile - Hunter Square
listings.content: Slick welcoming inexpensive hotel.

listings.name: Premier Inn Edinburgh City Centre
listings.content: Good reliable chain hotel by the station.

listings.name: Leonardo Royal Hotel
listings.content: Good value place next to the railway station.

listings.name: Ten Hill Place Hotel
listings.content: Central but quiet hotel in a Georgian terrace with 78 bedrooms.

listings.name: Holiday Inn Express
listings.content: They call it "Royal Mile" but it's in the dark canyon of Cowgate 200 yards south - still a very central location, and value for money.

listings.name: Edinburgh Holyrood Hotel
listings.content: Now part of Marriott chain, this is under renovation but remains open.

listings.name: Apex Grassmarket
listings.content: Comfy place to stay with great views of the castle.

listings.name: Apex City of Edinburgh
listings.content: Similar price and quality to their branch at No 31.

listings.name: Hotel du Vin
listings.content: Great comfort, service and location beyond its price bracket.

listings.name: Novotel
listings.content: Mid-range chain near Tolcross.

listings.name: DoubleTree by Hilton Hotel Edinburgh City Centre
listings.content: Comfy hotel near Usher Hall, short walk to the castle.

listings.name: The Scotsman
listings.content: This iconic building stands like a castle guarding the entrance to Old Town from North Bridge. From 1904 to 2001 it housed The Scotsman newspaper, with editors and reporters above, printing presses below, and newspapers loaded onto trains from the basement. After they moved out it became an upscale hotel, charmingly refurbished within and scoring highly for comfort, service and location.

listings.name: Hilton Edinburgh Carlton
listings.content: Great location, service and comfort mostly good, some construction noise.

listings.name: Sheraton Grand Hotel
listings.content: Part of Marriott chain, great location and for most visitors great comfort, but housekeeping is too erratic for what you pay.

listings.name: Radisson Blu Hotel
listings.content: Great location, comfort and service. The hotel was built in 1990, but with a retro-antique facade to blend with neighbouring buildings.

listings.name: Cheval Old Town Chambers
listings.content: This knock-through of medieval tenements was designed as luxury serviced apartments, but has added common areas to create a townhouse hotel.

listings.name: Radisson Collection Hotel
listings.content: Closed for refurbishment.

listings.name: Upright Gallery
listings.content: Small gallery of local artists' work.

listings.name: Royal Observatory
listings.content: This opened in 1896 to replace the observatory on Calton Hill in New Town (which remained active to 2009 but is now an art exhibition space). The ROE is owned by the Science and Technology Facilities Council and houses the University of Edinburgh's Institute for Astronomy. Public evenings in winter are on Tuesday (booking essential) with talks and tours of the site.

listings.name: Craigmillar Castle
listings.content: Extensive ruin of a medieval castle, built from the 14th century and abandoned in the 18th. Here was hatched the plot to murder Lord Darnley, the inconvenient husband of Mary Queen of Scots. He was blown up at Kirk O'Field (now the site of the university Old College) and when that didn't do the job he was smothered.

listings.name: Summerhall
listings.content: Contemporary art exhibitions and event venue in a confident Edwardian building, home of Royal (Dick) School of Veterinary Studies from 1916. In 2011 the vets moved out to Easter Bush campus, birthplace of Dolly the Sheep. See below for the distillery, brewery and pub within Summerhall.

listings.name: The Queen's Hall
listings.content: Performance space for musical events across all genres. The neo-classical building was a chapel from 1824 and converted to a concert hall in 1979, with a capacity of 900.

listings.name: Royal Commonwealth Pool
listings.content: The pool was built for the Commonwealth Games in 1970, and was used again for the 1986 and 2014 games.

listings.name: Dominion Cinema
listings.content: Art deco cinema opened in 1938 with plush leather sofas for an upscale experience.

listings.name: Midlothian Snowsports Centre
listings.content: This has a main slope of 400 m, a loop alongside, 3 nursery slopes, a chairlift and 2 tows. Equipment hire is available or bring your own. Wear long trousers, long sleeves and gloves as the dendrex matting will skin you when you fall. Some disruption as a restaurant and other facilities are being built, and limited parking.

listings.name: Susie's Vegetarian Kitchen
listings.content: Vegetarian wraps, burritos and burgers.

listings.name: The Wee Boulangerie
listings.content: Delicious French bakery for breads, croissants, baguettes and so on. Mostly takeaway but they have a few tables to sit in.

listings.name: Chaskaa
listings.content: Modern Indian restaurant, consistently high quality.

listings.name: Hendersons
listings.content: Renowned vegetarian restaurant, run by the family of the original Hendersons in Hanover St which was open from 1962-2020. Michelin gives it an entry in their guide.

listings.name: LeftField
listings.content: This cosy seafood bistro gets great reviews.

listings.name: Three Birds
listings.content: Fine dining with a classic British menu, but almost entirely GF and much is vegan.

listings.name: The Clay Oven
listings.content: Takeaway offering trad Indian cuisine, fully halal.

listings.name: Bakery Andante
listings.content: Small bakery chain with three other city outlets.

listings.name: Hermitage Bar
listings.content: This pub has very good food at reasonable prices and a pleasant modern interior.

listings.name: Voujon
listings.content: Reliable North Indian / Bangladeshi restaurant.

listings.name: Cask and Barrel
listings.content: Trad pub with a central horseshoe bar, good selection of ale and whisky. No food. They have another pub on Broughton St in New Town.

listings.name: Leslie's Bar
listings.content: A trad pub with charming 1890s interior, dog-friendly, changing guest ales and a decent selection of whiskies.

listings.name: Golf Tavern
listings.content: Good food and an outside seating area facing Bruntsfield Links. You can hire golf clubs and balls here to play on the Links.

listings.name: Canny Man's
listings.content: Famously idiosyncratic pub with quirky decor, excellent range of ales, impressive choice of wine and whisky, and decent food.

listings.name: Holyrood Distillery
listings.content: Small distillery making whisky, vodka, gin and rum. Established in 2019, their first whisky went on sale in 2023.

listings.name: Argyle Backpackers
listings.content: Mixed reviews, good facilities, definitely not a party hostel.

listings.name: University of Edinburgh Pollock Halls
listings.content: University student accommodation is available to others from last week in June to first week in September. Their main site is Pollock Halls, where you might be in Baird House, Chancellor's Court, Scholar's Hotel or Scott Hotel. They also run KM Hotel half a mile north at the edge of Old Town.

listings.name: Mortonhall Caravan & Camping Park
listings.content: Clean spacious site open all year, with good facilities and buses to town.

listings.name: The Bruntsfield
listings.content: Traditional hotel a 15 min walk to Old Town. Pets welcome.

listings.name: Southside Guest House
listings.content: This changed owners in 2022 and quality has dipped, but it's still a decent mid-price option.

listings.name: 94DR
listings.content: This 6-bedroom villa is now only available to book on an exclusive basis by the week, and no longer a standard B&B.

listings.name: Kingsway Guest House
listings.content: Smart friendly guest house in a quiet spot.

listings.name: Sonas Guest House
listings.content: Pleasant B&B in an 1870s villa. Parking for cars, but no motorbikes accepted.

listings.name: 23 Mayfield
listings.content: Outstanding B&B with 7 rooms in a smartly decorated Victorian house. No children under 7.

listings.name: Travelodge Cameron Toll
listings.content: Usual Travelodge chain experience, good value for what you pay.

listings.name: Prestonfield House
listings.content: On the site of a former monastery hence "Priestfield", this was built in 1687 as a country mansion, and is now an upscale hotel with 23 rooms near the foot of Arthur's Seat. Rave reviews for comfort, service and cuisine, and it often hosts events. Wedding parties should mind where they pose, as Highland cattle graze in its grounds.

listings.name: Royal Botanic Garden
listings.content: Impressive gardens with a large collection. Great place to wander around on a sunny day, or to sit and have a picnic. Highlights include the Rock Garden; the 165-m-long herbaceous border, backed by a huge, century-old beech hedge, and the Palm House, the tallest of its kind in Britain. The Palm House reopened in October 2026 after a big restoration, and you can only see it on pre-booked tours. (However all the other glasshouses are closed for rebuilding, and a small section of the garden is only open at weekends.) A number of sculptures, including two by Barbara Hepworth, are displayed around the gardens. The east gate has a bus service but the west gate is grander, with the John Hope Gateway building containing the restaurant, shop, and exhibitions. Botanic Cottage is an education centre in a house that was built in 1764-5, designed by John Adam and James Craig and moved to the garden in 2014. They also run the gardens at Benmore near Oban, Dawyck above Peebles, and Logan near Stranraer.
listings.address: Inverleith Row for East Gate, Arboretum Place for West Gate

listings.name: Patriothall Gallery
listings.content: Small art gallery and artists studios in the former co-op bakery. The gallery has regular exhibitions of modern art. The studios are open.on one weekend in mid-August and another in late November.

listings.name: Fettes College
listings.content: Boarding school in an impressive building in the style of a French Château by David Bryce built between 1863 and 1869. It can be seen from far away. Not open for tourists - the best view is looking through the fence from Carrington Road.

listings.name: Museum of Scottish Fire Heritage
listings.content: Volunteer-run museum within McDonald Road fire station. History of Scottish firefighting from the era of rival commercial fire companies, through early wooden fire engines to more recent appliances.

listings.name: Edinburgh Academicals
listings.content: "The Accies" were promoted in 2026 and now play rugby union in the Premiership, the amateur top tier in Scotland. Their home ground Raeburn Place (capacity 5000) staged the world's first rugby international on 27 March 1871. Scotland scored two tries and England scored one, so the result was 1-0 - a "try" in those days only gave you a chance to kick at goal.

listings.name: The Grange
listings.content: This is the usual home ground for the Scottish national team, the Saltires. They play 50-over and 20-over matches but not five-day Tests. Gen!us Grange play in the domestic leagues.

listings.name: Glenogle Swim Centre
listings.content: Council-run Victorian swimming pool with partial glass roof. Also has a gym and sauna.

listings.name: King George V Park
listings.content: Park with a couple of children's play areas and many quiet benches to sit on. A path through an old railway tunnel links the park with Cannonmills Tesco, making this an ideal lunch spot.

listings.name: Inverleith Park
listings.content: Large park with several sports pitches for rugby, football and cricket, and public tennis courts. The south of the park has a pond divided into a wildlife area popular with swans, and a boating pond which is often used for model boats. The banked area near the pond offers good views over the New Town of the Castle, and there is a small floral area in the Sundial Garden.

listings.name: The Bailie
listings.content: Lovely old trad basement pub, known as much for its ale as its food. Standard pub-grub menu, but quality and prices are a notch higher.

listings.name: Avery
listings.content: Innovative Scots fare in a restaurant with one Michelin Star.

listings.name: The Raeburn
listings.content: Restaurant, pub, beer garden and small hotel in a house built in 1832.

listings.name: Scran and Scallie
listings.content: Upmarket gastro pub with modern Scots cuisine, slick service. They also run the Michelin-starred Kitchin in Leith.

listings.name: Eòrna
listings.content: Rave reviews for their Scottish fine dining. The name means "barley".

listings.name: The Orchard
listings.content: Friendly pub with bar meals, including gluten free.

listings.name: Mimi's Bakehouse
listings.content: Stockbridge branch of an Edinburgh chain of cafés, serving a fairly standard range of sandwiches, but interesting seasonal cakes and bakes.

listings.name: Little Parlour
listings.content: About 30 flavours of ice cream from Stewart Tower in Perthshire, and a selection of confectionery. The shop was opened as a Gentemen's Hairdressers in 1896 and continued as a barbers until 2024; the shop has only had small alterations for its present use.

listings.name: The Stockbridge Tap
listings.content: Trad bar with a good range of ales and whiskies, and a limited food selection.

listings.name: Ardenlee Guest House
listings.content: Pleasant Victorian terrace B&B half a mile from Princes Street.

listings.name: Canon Court Aparthotel
listings.content: Offers a wide range or 1- and 2-bedroom serviced apartments for short term lettings, in a building near the Water of Leith.

listings.name: Village Hotel Club
listings.content: Chain hotel in an ugly black box building, comfy enough. The main draw is the large gym and pool, non-residents can get day passes for this. It has a car park (£5 per day midweek), restaurant and bar, and frequent buses into town.

listings.name: Brig O' Doon Guest House
listings.content: Cosy friendly B&B by Goldenacres sports ground. Frequent buses to town centre. It's owned by Ardleigh House next door, which gets poor reviews and is overpriced.

listings.name: Edinburgh Printmakers
listings.content: Creative centre for printmaking & visual arts, Two free galleries & shop. Vegan Cafe.

listings.name: Edinburgh Zoo
listings.content: The pandas have returned to China but there's still plenty here. Penguins include gentoo, rockhopper and king, most famously Major General Sir Nils Olav III, Baron of the Bouvet Islands and mascot of the Norwegian King's Guard. Budongo Trail leads through the troupe of 15 chimpanzees. The only koalas in the UK are here, and there are some beautiful tropical birds. The zoo is on the slopes of Corstorphine Hill and some paths are steep but all attractions are wheelchair accessible. Check the website for cheaper online offers, and temporary closures eg in harsh weather or avian flu outbreaks.

listings.name: Corstorphine Old Parish Church
listings.content: The present building is a collegiate church of 1429, becoming a parish church in 1646, and re-modeled in 1828.

listings.name: Lauriston Castle
listings.content: This 1590s tower house was extended in the 1820s and housed a series of prosperous families. It passed into council ownership in 1926 and the interior has been preserved in its last occupants' plush Edwardian style. Visit by pre-booked guided tour. There is free entry to the gardens (daily 8AM-4:30PM), where the centrepiece is the Japanese garden. The castle is also used as an event space.

listings.name: Murrayfield Stadium
listings.content: The main stadium has a capacity of 67,000 and hosts all Scottish rugby internationals. The premier tournament is the Six Nations held each February-March: in odd-numbered years, Scotland hosts Wales, Ireland and Italy, and in even-numbered years the visitors are England and France. These games almost always sell out, and the city is mobbed when they're on; you've more chance of tickets and accommodation for other internationals which take place each November, or, if it's a Rugby World Cup year, warm-up friendly games in the summer. Stadium tours are available on non-match days.

listings.name: Murrayfield Ice Rink
listings.content: Popular ice rink with leisure skating sessions, and ice-discos on Friday and Saturday nights. It's the home rink of the Edinburgh Capitals ice hockey team, who play Sept-March in the Scottish National League, the UK second tier. (Their rivals Murrayfield Racers folded in 2022.) The curling club also play here on a separate rink.

listings.name: Cineworld
listings.content: Mainly mainstream cinema with some art-house & foreign cinema. IMAX screen.

listings.name: Royal Highland Showground
listings.content: An exhibition ground with several halls and large grounds. The premier event is the Royal Highland Show for 4 days in late June. Other events are held throughout the year, some of these are public, others are trade only.

listings.name: Edinburgh International Climbing Arena
listings.content: Huge indoor and outdoor climbing centre in a disused quarry, developed from 1995 but taken over and completed by Edinburgh City Council in 2007.

listings.name: Heart of Midlothian
listings.content: Hearts aka "the Jambos" and "the Gorgie Boys" play soccer in the Scottish Premiership, the top tier. Their home ground Tynecastle Park (capacity 20,000, all-seater) is a mile west of Haymarket station in the Gorgie area of the city; take any bus up Gorgie Road or a tram to Murrayfield.

listings.name: Spartans
listings.content: The Spartans play soccer in Scottish League Two, the fourth tier. Their ground Ainslie Park (Vanloq Community Stadium) holds 3612, of which 534 are seated. It's in Pilton, northwest of the city centre.

listings.name: Edinburgh Filmhouse
listings.content: A four-screen Edinburgh institution showing largely arthouse and some mainstream films. Additionally houses a 100-seat cafe-bar.
listings.price: £12 adult, £10.50 concession, wheelchair users/access tickets £5, carers free

listings.name: First Coast
listings.content: Long-standing bistro serving quality Scots cuisine.

listings.name: Masti
listings.content: Classic North Indian Balti menu.

listings.name: Miller & Carter Cramond Brig
listings.content: Popular chain steakhouse getting great reviews. The old Cramond Brig is now a footbridge over River Almond, follow the east bank for the village and island, and the west bank to hike to South Queensferry. Modern traffic thunders past on A90.

listings.name: Holy Cow Lounge
listings.content: Vegan cafe in Edinburgh Printmakers building.

listings.name: The Murrayfield
listings.content: Friendly pub close to Murrayfield Stadium with screens for TV sport. Decent all-day pub grub.

listings.name: Cramond Inn
listings.content: Traditional village pub run by Samuel Smiths. Beer garden outside but food service is indoors-only. No dogs.

listings.name: Bainfield
listings.content: This is single-room student accommodation for Napier University but available to others during the summer break.

listings.name: Holiday Inn Edinburgh
listings.content: Simple value hotel with restaurant. Those strange noises are from the zoo animals next door.

listings.name: Holiday Inn Express Edinburgh City West
listings.content: Acceptable rooms, variable welcome and service.

listings.name: White Lady
listings.content: Small hotel on the Glasgow Rd run by JD Wetherspoon. Frequent buses to city centre.

listings.name: Leonardo
listings.content: Value-for-money hotel on Corstorphine Hill, calls itself "Murrayfield" which is two miles southeast.

listings.name: Bridge Inn
listings.content: On the canal, and most customers are just here for the excellent dining, but the snug rooms are well worth a stay. Closed for maintenance until March 2024.

listings.name: Hampton by Hilton Edinburgh Airport
listings.content: The closest to the terminal, a 300 yard walk, this is comfy and efficient.

listings.name: Doubletree by Hilton Edinburgh Airport
listings.content: Comfy hotel a 10-minute walk from the terminal.

listings.name: Moxy Edinburgh Airport
listings.content: Modern hotel with small, comfortable rooms and friendly staff. It's a 10-minute walk from the terminal - head for the trams, then follow the signs pointing to the Doubletree Hotel.

listings.name: Holiday Inn Express
listings.content: A bit frayed but overall good value. It's by the Showground, a 20-minute walk from the terminal so take their shuttle bus.

listings.name: Travelodge Edinburgh Airport
listings.content: Value hotel two miles west of airport with shuttle bus.
listings.address: Ratho Park, off Station Rd, Ratho Station EH28 8PP

listings.name: Premier Inn Edinburgh Airport
listings.content: Reliable chain hotel three miles west of airport with shuttle bus.

listings.name: The Roseate
listings.content: Mixed reviews - the main building is okay, but some rooms are in a basement across the road and not worth the money.

listings.name: Novotel Edinburgh Park
listings.content: Unlovely area of light industry and retail, but the hotel is next to M8 / city bypass interchange and Edinburgh Park Station. It has a pool, gym, steam room and restaurant.

listings.name: Norton House Hotel
listings.content: Villa built in 1840 as country retreat, and now a hotel and spa in woodland close to the airport. Great welcome and service, smart modern interior. It's 10 mins walk to main bus routes on the road to Glasgow, but you really ought to be arriving by limo or helicopter. It hosts a lot of functions for people who wished they were.

listings.name: Dalmahoy
listings.content: Grand pile built in 1725 and much extended since, it's now an upscale hotel and golf resort.
